name: Khmer nationalism
summary: Khmer nationalism holds that the Khmers are a distinct people and nation, heirs of Angkor, whose language, culture, Buddhism and territory must be defended and revived. Its constant theme is the Vietnamese (and to a lesser degree Thai) as the hereditary threat, with grievance over Kampuchea Krom and distrust of the Vietnamese minority. Its strands differ on the monarchy: royalist (Sihanouk, the 1993 Kingdom), republican (Son Ngoc Thanh, Lon Nol) and communist (the Khmer Rouge).
scope: The doctrine on the national question (identity, territory, sovereignty, language, culture, minorities, kin abroad, means) from the 1930s Nagaravatta circle of Son Ngoc Thanh through the Sangkum, Lon Nol's neo-Khmerism and the Khmer Republic, Democratic Kampuchea's nationalist texts (Black Paper) and today's nationalism of the CPP and the opposition. Based on the Black Paper, Pol Pot's 1977 speech for its national lines only, the 1993 constitution's nation-defining articles, Mak and Heder. The economic, social and regime-form programmes of the Sangkum, the Khmer Republic, DK and the CPP are not part of it and are null unless the nationalist texts state them as part of the national cause. Lon Nol's New Khmerism and Sihanouk's speeches could not be read in full.

sources.usedFor: Khmer territorial claims (Kampuchea Krom), the view of Vietnam as an annexing neighbour, land ownership by foreigners, sovereignty and non-interference. Read in Swedish, in full.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: DK and Chhak treat Vietnamese annexation of Kampuchea Krom as illegal, while the 1993 constitution takes the present borders as final; strands differ.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: The Black Paper cites Khmer inhabitants of Tay Ninh and Song Be as a ground for Khmer territorial claims and DK armed the Khmer Krom, but the 1993 constitution fixes the border, so the strands split.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Sarin Chhak's thesis (foreword by Sihanouk) and the DK border paper held the colonial decrees that ceded Khmer land void, while the 1993 constitution accepts the colonial-era map as the frontier, so strands differ.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Mak documents Khmer racial and national exceptionalism in the nationalism of Lon Nol and DK, with the Vietnamese cast as barbaric aggressors, which does not treat cultures as merely different.

defeat-communism.rationale: The Khmer Republic fought the communists as a threat to the Khmer race and the Sangkum suppressed the left, while the Khmer Rouge and the Khmer Issarak were communist nationalists, so strands split.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Royalist Khmer nationalism passes the throne within the royal family (the 1993 constitution has a council pick a king), while the republican and DK strands reject hereditary headship; the strands split.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Nagaravatta attacked Vietnamese and Chinese domination of the civil service and economy, and the Khmer Republic blamed the Chinese for sabotaging the national economy.

elective-rulers.rationale: Royalist nationalism has the throne inherited, while the republican strand (Thanh, Lon Nol) wants rulers chosen by election; Heder records the two as divergent streams.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Heder describes the twentieth-century project as an exclusivist, monolithic Khmer nation: Lon Nol's 'great Khmer race' excluding Vietnamese and Chinese, and DK's single Khmer nationality.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Article 44 of the 1993 constitution gives land ownership only to Khmer-nationality persons and entities, and the Black Paper states that Kampuchean law has never let foreigners acquire land and condemns Vietnamese who did.

historical-land-claim.rationale: The Black Paper and Lon Nol's New Khmerism ground the claim to Kampuchea Krom in Khmer settlement there for two thousand years, against the Vietnamese who settled later; Mak calls the sentiment widely shared.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: The 1993 constitution makes defending the motherland a duty of every citizen and the preamble commits to defend Cambodia's territory, and Pol Pot's speech calls for defending the national territory from coast to coast; a spiritual bond itself is not spelled out.

keep-colonial-borders.rationale: The 1993 constitution keeps the borders mapped in 1933-1953, while DK and Chhak rejected colonial boundaries as unlawful; the strands split.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Nationalist regimes classed Khmer in Vietnam and Thailand as Khmer Kraom and Khmer Surin, which Heder calls implicitly irredentist, and the Black Paper counts the Khmer Krom among the nation, so language and ancestry bound the nation across borders.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Lon Nol and DK justified attacks on ethnic Vietnamese as targeting agents of a Vietnamese plot, DK called the Khmer-born 'Vietnamese minds in Khmer bodies', and opposition rallies since 2013 voice the same suspicion.

minority-language-support.rationale: The Sangkum and the Khmer Republic Khmerized the minorities and restricted Chinese schooling, DK banned other languages, and nationalists see officially sanctioned multiculturalism as a worry.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Sihanouk's circle saw the Cambodian nation as intrinsically royal and the 1993 motto is Nation, Religion, King, but Son Ngoc Thanh's republican current, Lon Nol's republic and DK rejected the monarchy, so the strands split.

national-church-status.rationale: The Sangkum made protection of Buddhism a main theme and the 1993 constitution says Buddhism shall be the religion of the State, within a motto of Nation, Religion, King.

national-rebirth.rationale: Heder describes the nationalist projects as redemptionist ones to relaunch Cambodia as a glorious nation, Lon Nol promised an accelerated programme to restore Angkorian glory, and DK sought to lift the 'national soul'.

national-self-determination.rationale: Anti-colonial Khmer nationalism from Nagaravatta on demanded independence for the Khmer nation, and both DK's constitution and the 1993 constitution proclaim an independent, sovereign state.

native-born-offices.rationale: The nationalists' Khmerization drive displaced Vietnamese officials from the civil service, and the 1993 constitution requires National Assembly candidates to hold Khmer nationality at birth.

population-transfer.rationale: Lon Nol's army expelled 200,000 to 250,000 Vietnamese and DK deported about 150,000, but the Sangkum and the post-1993 state did not, so only two regimes are documented.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Heder shows preserving and reviving Khmer culture and tradition as the core of every strand from Nagaravatta to today, and the 1993 constitution's preamble commits to the prestige of the Angkor civilization.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: The Black Paper denounces the persecution of the Khmer Krom, DK armed Khmer Krom guerrillas, and Khmer Krom and Khmer Surin are named as part of the nation; Mak calls the irredentist feeling widely shared among Cambodians.

racial-pride.rationale: Lon Nol's state propaganda and war aims centred on the 'great Khmer race', and Mak describes a Khmer chauvinism of racial exceptionalism shared by Lon Nol and DK.

return-lost-territory.rationale: DK, Lon Nol's New Khmerism and the Sihanouk-era claim to Kampuchea Krom demanded its return, but the 1993 constitution fixes Cambodia's borders on the 1933-1953 map, so the strands split.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: DK and the Khmer Republic sought to recover Kampuchea Krom and unite the Khmer, but the later royal and CPP-era state accepts its present borders, so the strands split.

right-to-secede.rationale: The 1993 constitution declares the state indivisible and its territory inviolable, and DK's constitution and Pol Pot's speech affirm territorial integrity coast to coast, so a right of regions to secede is not part of the doctrine.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Preserving inherited Khmer culture and the glory of Angkor is central to the nationalists and the 1993 preamble, which is at odds with sacrificing heritage for new creation.

separate-church-state.rationale: A state religion (Buddhism) and the Nation, Religion, King motto cannot stand with strict separation of religion and state, and the Sangkum made protecting Buddhism a theme of its nationalism.

single-official-language.rationale: Khmerization of the state and of schooling has been the common cause from Nagaravatta through the Sangkum, Khmer Republic and DK to the CPP (Khmer is the constitutional official language), and nationalists resist bilingual schooling.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: The early nationalists wanted to be modern by being more like the Khmer of old, and Lon Nol's neo-Khmerism paired traditional culture with a special accelerated economic programme.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Pol Pot's speech says the people have lived in the same territory for over two thousand years with their own history and Angkor, the Black Paper treats Kampuchea Krom as Khmer for two millennia, and the 1993 preamble calls Cambodians heirs of a great civilization.

missingStatements.text: Settlement by a neighbouring people on a country's territory is a form of annexation by stealth.
missingStatements.rationale: The Black Paper describes Vietnamese settlement in Prey Nokor and along the Mekong as the method by which Vietnam swallowed Kampuchea Krom and meant to swallow Kampuchea.

missingStatements.text: The civil service and the economy should be cleared of people of a neighbouring or immigrant nationality and placed in the hands of the nation's own people.
missingStatements.rationale: Nagaravatta pressed the Khmerization of the civil service against Vietnamese officials and attacked Chinese economic domination, and the Khmer Republic repeated the line.

notes: Strands: royalist (Sangkum, 1993 Kingdom), republican (Son Ngoc Thanh, Lon Nol), communist (the Khmer Rouge) and the modern CPP and opposition; they split on the monarchy, on Kampuchea Krom (claimed by DK, Lon Nol and the early Sihanouk state, fixed away by the 1993 constitution) and on communism. Positions on economy, welfare, social policy and foreign alignment belong to the regimes and parties, not to the nationalist doctrine, and are null. Themes searched: culture, language, minorities, territory, sovereignty, citizenship and land, religion, monarchy. Not readable: Lon Nol's New Khmerism and Sihanouk's speeches themselves (only Mak and Heder report them); Pol Pot's speech is a blog copy of the Liberator Press translation. The Black Paper is DK's harshest strand.
